1717688.title: Mottisfont Abbey
1717688.extract: Mottisfont Abbey is a historical priory and country estate in Hampshire, England. Sheltered in the valley of the River Test, the property is now operated by the National Trust. 393,250 people visited the site in 2019. The site includes the historic house museum which features regularly changing art exhibitions, gardens, including a walled rose garden which is home to the National Plant Collection of ancestral rose species and 19th-century rose cultivars, and a riverside walk. It is a Grade I listed building.

'''Mottisfont Abbey''' is a historical [[priory]] and [[English country house|country]] [[Estate (land)|estate]] in [[Hampshire]], [[England]]. Sheltered in the [[valley]] of the [[River Test]], the property is now operated by the [[National Trust]]. 393,250 people visited the site in 2019.<ref name="ALVA 2019 visitor numbers">{{cite web |title=ALVA - Association of Leading Visitor Attractions |url=https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423 |website=www.alva.org.uk |access-date=27 October 2020}}</ref> The site includes the [[historic house museum]] which features regularly changing art exhibitions, gardens, including a walled [[rose garden]] which is home to the [[National Plant Collection]] of ancestral rose species and 19th-century rose cultivars,<ref name=":0">Stone, D. (2008). Pruning Roses. In: The National Trust, ed., ''Gardening Secrets from National Trust Head Gardeners'' (pp. 49-52). London: National Trust Books. {{ISBN|978-1-905400-35-5}}.</ref> and a riverside walk. It is a Grade I [[listed building]].<ref>{{NHLE |desc=Mottisfont Abbey House|num=1093730|access-date=15 November 2018}}</ref>

==History==

=== Priory ===
Fertile land and a plentiful water supply attracted the first settlers. The site's name comes from a spring ("[[Fountain|font]]") that is still producing water in the grounds. It was the font around which the local community held its [[Thing (assembly)|moots]] or meetings. An [[Augustinians|Augustinian]] [[priory]] was founded here in 1201 by [[William Brewer (justice)|William Briwere]], a businessman, administrator and courtier to four [[Plantagenet]] kings who chose to make a public demonstration of his wealth and piety. The canons welcomed [[pilgrim]]s en route to [[Winchester Cathedral|Winchester]], who came to worship Mottisfont's [[relic]], said to be the finger of St [[John the Baptist]].

Struck by the [[Black Death]], the initially prosperous priory suffered from the mid-14th century onwards. Its landholdings included the church at [[Berwick St James]], Wiltshire.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|author-last1=Baggs|author-first1=A. P.|url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/wilts/vol15/pp168-177|title=A History of the County of Wiltshire, Volume 15|author-last2=Freeman|author-first2=Jane|author-last3=Stevenson|author-first3=Janet H.|date=1995|publisher=University of London|editor-last=Crowley|editor-first=D. A.|series=[[Victoria County History]]|pages=168–177|chapter=Parishes: Berwick St James|access-date=23 October 2021|via=British History Online}}</ref>

=== House ===
During the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]] under [[Henry VIII]], the priory was dissolved and in 1536 the King gave Mottisfont to a favoured statesman, Sir [[William Sandys, 1st Baron Sandys|William Sandys]] (died 1540),<ref name=":1" /> who turned it into a country home but, rather unusually, chose not to demolish the existing priory. Sandys instead turned the church [[nave]] into the main body of the new mansion, building additional wings on either side. Sections of the original medieval church may still be seen, with the later additions built around them. The 13th-century [[wikt:cellarium|cellarium]] also remains present today.

In the 18th century, the old monastic cloisters and Tudor courtyard were demolished by the Mill family, creating the modern appearance of the house's [[facade]]. 
[[File:Mottifont in 2023.jpg|thumb|left|Mottisfont main building May 2023]]
It was at this time that the owners added "Abbey" to the name of the house rather than the more historically correct "Priory". The National Trust speculates that the name was considered to be more romantic.<ref name="NT Mottisford: Mill family">{{cite web | title = Meet the Mills at Mottisfont | publisher = National Trust | url = http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/article-1356395273972/ | access-date = 8 Feb 2014}}</ref> Under Sir [[John Barker-Mill]], in the early 19th century, the estate became a centre for hunting, shooting and fishing, and a new [[stable]] block was built.<ref name="NT Mottisford: Mill family" />
The last decades of the 19th century saw Mottisfont let to wealthy banker Daniel Meinertzhagen under eccentric terms that forbade the installation of electric light or [[central heating]]. The ten Meinertzhagen children included Daniel and [[Richard Meinertzhagen|Richard]], who built [[Aviary|aviaries]] for their collection of [[eagle]]s, [[hawk]]s, [[owl]]s and [[raven]]s. Richard wrote detailed diaries about his childhood and growing interest in the natural world.<ref name="Guide">{{cite book |last1=Moore |first1=Cathal |last2=Thomas |first2=Graham Stuart |title=Mottisfont Abbey |date=1996 |publisher=National Trust |location=Swindon |pages=11–13}}</ref>

=== 20th century ===
[[File:Angel Mosaic.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Angel Mosaic by Boris Anrep]]
The arrival of [[Maud Julia Augusta Russell|Maud]] and [[Gilbert Byng Alwyne Russell|Gilbert Russell]] in 1934 made Mottisfont the centre of a fashionable artistic and political circle. Maud was a wealthy patron of the arts, and she created a substantial country house where she entertained artists and writers including [[Ben Nicholson]] and [[Ian Fleming]]. She commissioned some of her artist and designer friends to embellish Mottisfont, always with an eye on its history, which fascinated her. [[Rex Whistler]] created the illusion of [[Gothic architecture]] in her [[Drawing room|salon]] (now known as the Whistler Room), a piece of [[trompe-l'œil]] painting that recalls the medieval architecture of the priory. [[Boris Anrep]] contributed mosaics both inside and outside the house, including one of an angel featuring Maud's face – the couple had a long love affair.{{Citation needed|date=November 2018}}

During [[World War II]], Mottisfont was commandeered as a hospital with 80 beds.<ref name=Guide />

Maud Russell gave the house and grounds to the [[National Trust]] in 1957, although continuing to live there until 1972.<ref name="NT Mottisford: Russell family">{{cite web | title = Meet the Russells at Mottisfont | publisher = National Trust | url = http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/article-1356395271117/ | access-date = 8 Feb 2014}}</ref> One of the artists who had visited regularly was [[Derek Hill (painter)|Derek Hill]], a society portrait painter who had a private passion for [[landscape painting]], and who collected work by his contemporaries. He donated a substantial collection of early 20th-century art to the National Trust to be shown at Mottisfont, in memory of his long friendship with Maud Russell. Today, these works are joined by a changing programme of temporary exhibitions of 20th-century and contemporary art.

==Burials==
*[[Maud Chaworth]]{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}, 14th-century noblewoman and heiress

==Visitor attraction==
[[Image:Mottisfont Abbey Gardens1a.UME.jpg|right|thumb|Mottisfont Abbey gardens]]
[[File:Mottisfont Rose Garden, Mottisfont Abbey.JPG|thumb|Mottisfont Rose Garden]]
[[Image:Mottisfont Abbey Estate Walk.jpg|thumb|A map of the estate walk]]
Mottisfont Abbey has extensive grounds. There are areas of wooded shade, a walk along the [[River Test]], enough lawn for picnics, and games are allowed on the lawns, too. 
There is the largest specimen of a [[Platanus × hispanica|London plane]] tree in Britain.

Mottisford is home to the Plant Heritage [[National Plant Collection]] ''Rosa'' (pre-1900 [[shrub rose]]). The roses reach their peak in June and are scented, particularly on early summer evenings.<ref name=":0" />

In the summer months there are often theatre productions outside, and at different times of the year there are specific trails, mainly but not exclusively aimed at children, for example at Easter, Halloween, Christmas etc.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

Refreshments are sold at several points and there is a modern National Trust shop, ice cream parlour and exhibition space. A new Visitor Centre was completed early in 2016. An environmentally friendly building, it is heated in winter months by a biomass boiler burning wood-chips from the estate.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

From The [[Test Way]], which passes through Mottisfont and around the Abbey grounds, the main house is seen from the rear as you pass through fields along the northern boundary.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

1891739.title: The Vyne
1891739.extract:
The Vyne is a Grade I listed 16th-century country house in the parish of Sherborne St John, near Basingstoke, in Hampshire, England. The house was first built circa 1500–10 in the Tudor style by William Sandys, 1st Baron Sandys, Lord Chamberlain to King Henry VIII. In the 17th century it was transformed to resemble a classical mansion. Today, although much reduced in size, the house retains its Tudor chapel, with contemporary stained glass. The classical portico on the north front was added in 1654 to the design of John Webb, a pupil of Inigo Jones, and is notable as the first portico in English domestic architecture.
In the mid-18th century the house belonged to John Chaloner Chute, a close friend of the architectural pioneer Horace Walpole, who designed the principal stair hall containing an imperial staircase the grand scale of which belies its true small size. In 1958 The Vyne was bequeathed by Charles Chute to the National Trust.

'''The Vyne''' is a [[Grade I listed]]<ref>{{NHLE|grade=I|desc=The Vyne|num= 1296972|date=26 April 1957}}</ref> 16th-century [[country house]] in the parish of [[Sherborne St John]], near [[Basingstoke]], in [[Hampshire]], [[England]]. The house was first built ''circa'' 1500–10 in the Tudor style by [[William Sandys, 1st Baron Sandys]], [[Lord Chamberlain]] to King [[Henry VIII]]. In the 17th century it was transformed to resemble a classical mansion. Today, although much reduced in size, the house retains its [[The Vyne Chapel|Tudor chapel]], with contemporary stained glass. The classical [[portico]] on the north front was added in 1654 to the design of [[John Webb (architect)|John Webb]], a pupil of [[Inigo Jones]], and is notable as the first portico in English domestic architecture.

In the mid-18th century the house belonged to John Chaloner Chute, a close friend of the architectural pioneer [[Horace Walpole]], who designed the principal stair hall containing an [[imperial staircase]] the grand scale of which belies its true small size. In 1958 The Vyne was bequeathed by [[Charles Chute]] to the [[National Trust]].

== Nomenclature ==
The Vyne stands on the site of a medieval manor house of the same name. The origins of the name, earliest preserved on a document dated 1268,<ref name=howard42>Howard, p. 42.</ref> are uncertain; one theory suggests that it refers to ''Vindomis'', a Roman road station,<ref>Nicolson, p. 44.</ref> whilst another that it was the site of the first domestically grown vines in England.{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=11}} In its early history the house and its precincts were often referred to as "The Vyne Green", possibly because the small manor house, its detached chapel and assorted outbuildings were arranged around a square, much like a [[village green]].{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=12}} This assortment of buildings was gradually linked to form one large dwelling, the origins of the present house.

== History ==
In the fourteenth century the house then on the site was the manor house of Sherborne Cowdray, [[Feudal land tenure in England|held]] by the Fyffhide family.<ref name=howard42/> Following the death of Sir William Fyffhide the manor was leased to Gregory of Basingstoke until 1370, when the house was described as comprising "a [[Great hall|hall]], adjoining chambers and the grange and chapel at the house."<ref name=howard42/>

In 1386 the manor passed by marriage into the Sandys family; in 1420, again by marriage, it passed to the Brocas family, and in 1488 returned to Sandys,{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=43}} the family most closely associated with the early history of the mansion. The Sandys family rose to prominence during the reign of King Henry VIII, and was founded by [[William Sandys, 1st Baron Sandys]], a royal servant and courtier, who served as [[Lord Chamberlain]] from 1526 until his death in 1540.{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=41}} He transformed the medieval manor house into a vast mansion befitting his exalted rank.{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=10}} Successive generations of the Sandys family held the manor. [[William Sandys, 3rd Baron Sandys]] (d. 1623) entertained Queen Elizabeth I at the house twice, in 1569 and 1601.{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=13}} Having joined the insurrection of the Earl of Essex he was imprisoned and fined £5,000, when the house passed temporarily into the hands of the crown.<ref>Howard, p. 47.</ref> Although the house was restored to the Sandys family, their fortunes entered decline and no member was to hold high office again. During the Civil War the house was the residence of the Cavalier Colonel Henry Sandys and following the fall of nearby [[Basing House]], a Royalist stronghold, the Vyne was occupied by Parliamentarians.{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1959|p=7}} Colonel Sandys died of his wounds following the [[Battle of Cheriton]] and nine years later, in 1653, his son William 6th Baron sold The Vyne to [[Chaloner Chute]], a prosperous lawyer and later MP.{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1959|p=7}}{{efn|William 6th Baron retired to [[Mottisfont Abbey]], which had been acquired and developed by his ancestor William 1st Baron.{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1959|p=–67}}}}

===The Chute family===
The Chute family were to own The Vyne from 1653 until the mid twentieth century, and it is they who are largely responsible for the house as it appears today. The Vyne's purchaser, Challoner Chute, chosen Speaker of the House of Commons on 27 Jan 1659, instigated at The Vyne a program of demolition and rebuilding, sweeping away much of the Sandys' great Tudor mansion and transforming what remained into a smaller classical house.{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=14}} At first glance, Chute's chosen style resembles [[Palladianism]]; a form of architecture which had briefly been popular on England before the Civil War, but following the cessation of the war had been dismissed as Royalist. Indeed, [[Inigo Jones]] who had introduced the style to the English court had been captured at the fall of nearby Basing House, and taken prisoner, naked and humiliated, from the house as it was looted. {{sfn|Gardiner|1889|p=346}} So it is surprising that Chute, a prominent Parliamentarian, chose to rebuild his house in an unfashionable style, but also chose as his architect, [[John Webb (architect)|John Webb]], a former pupil of Jones.{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=42}}

In the 18th century, Chaloner's descendant John Chute{{efn|His inheritance was unexpected as he was the youngest of ten children.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=78}}}} undertook significant renovations to the house, including a new interior to the chapel, the construction of the tomb and the installation of the staircase.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=80}} John's Chute's design choices were influenced by the ideas of his friend Horace Walpole, with whom he became acquainted while staying at the home of Horace Mann in Florence in the 1740s.{{sfn|Tipping|1921|p=642}} He died childless in 1776{{sfn|Tipping|1921|p=646}} and the estate passed to his cousin Thomas Lobb, who took the name Chute.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=80}} Lobb made no significant alterations during his ownership of the house.{{sfn|Tipping|1921|p=647}} He was likewise without heir and again the inheritance was settled in 1837 on a cousin named William Wiggett, who also took the name Chute.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=80}}  William Wigget's renovation efforts on the estate were focused on the farmland and the roof rather than the interior of the house{{sfn|Tipping|1921|p=648-649}} On his death in 1879 the house passed to his son Chaloner W. Chute.{{sfn|Tipping|1921|p=649}}

In 1888 Chaloner W. Chute published ''A History of The Vyne'', covering the story of the estate, its occupants and collections through the centuries. The house remained in the Chute family until it was given to the National Trust in 1956{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=16}} by Sir Charles Chute.{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1959|p=9}} His bequest included the house, its contents and 1124 acres of land, along with an endowment.{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1959|p=9}}

== Architecture ==

===16th century===
[[File:The Stone Gallery.jpg|thumb|alt=A Tudor long gallery, with stone floors, wooden furniture and bust sculpture|The southern end of the Stone Gallery]]
Precise details of William Sandys new house at The Vyne are vague. Recent archaeological research at the site has indicated a vast mansion spreading northwest from the present house, built around four courtyards – this would be consistent with better documented houses also belonging to high ranking Tudor courtiers. The author Maurice Howard in his book, The Vyne, suggests that the house, may have rivalled [[Hampton Court]], the palace of the King's favourite, [[Cardinal Wolsey]].<ref>Howard, p. 44.</ref> This view seems to be confirmed in the writings of the sixteenth century antiquarian [[John Leland (antiquary)|John Leland]] who described the house as "''one of the most princely houses in goodly building in all Hampshire.''"<ref>Leland, quoted by Nicolson, p. 44.</ref>

Work began in 1500 and it can be reliably assumed that by 1510 The Vyne was a sizeable and comfortable mansion because in that year Sandys entertained King Henry VIII during his royal progress.{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=52}}{{efn|Henry visited again in 1535 with Anne Boleyn, the year before her execution.{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1959|p=9}}}}  An inventory drawn up in 1541 describes the house as having 57 "named rooms" – implying there were innumerable more nameless rooms.{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=18}} Of the rooms named and known was a [[long gallery]], one of the earliest of such galleries to be found in an English house – the house also contained a series of small parlours and bedrooms which afforded the house's occupants a degree of privacy not common in Tudor houses at the time.<ref name=Nicolson47>Nicolson, p. 47.</ref> Much of the fine [[linenfold]] panelling which lined these rooms remains today still in situ in the oldest parts of the house.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=78}}

===17th century===
[[File:Vineexpirement.jpg|thumb|Ground floor plan.]]
[[File:Vyne2.jpg|thumb|First floor plan.]]
Immediately upon purchase, Chute embarked on a radical redesign, by sweeping away the Base Court of the former house and all its precincts to the north – the area occupied by lawns and the lake today. Leaving only one wing of the Sandys' house containing the Long Gallery, the hall and reception rooms. The Tudor asymmetrical mullioned windows were removed and replaced by classical rectangular windows in stone frames, these pierced the walls at regular intervals providing near, but not precise symmetry. At the centre of the north front, Webb created a portico, the first of its kind on a private house in England.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=78}} The instant appearance was Palladian – yet this is not really the case – in no way did it resemble the Palladianism of Charles I's reign, exemplified by the [[Banqueting House, Whitehall]] and the [[Queen's House, Greenwich]], or even the later Palladianism pioneered by [[Richard Boyle, 3rd Earl of Burlington|Lord Burlington]] where the portico was an essential feature was still seventy years away.

Even if Webb had wished to create a truly Palladian house in the spirit of Inigo Jones, conversion from a Tudor house, rather than complete rebuilding rendered Palladianism impossible. The nature of the existing building confined Webb's classicising to attempting a cohesion and unity appearance rather than design. One of the greatest obstacles to any attempt at true symmetry was the blue [[diapering]] the red Tudor brickwork, this created huge lozenge patterns in the walls which could never symmetrically match the newly installed even placed windows.

Webb's portico is built of rendered brick with [[Corinthian order|Corinthian]] capitals of [[Burford]] stone.<ref name=howard7>Howard, p. 7.</ref> Its design, however, has anomalies, which are not consistent with the work of such an experienced architect. It has "abrupt" side opening; these are rectangular and bricked rather than more conventionally arched and plastered while the pediment itself is made of painted wood rather than stone. The architectural commentator [[Nigel Nicolson]] advocates a view that the portico was not finished as Webb intended.<ref>Nicolson, p. 48.</ref> Whatever the architectural merits of the portico, it is important as the first on any English house. The impression of symmetrical Palladianism was further enforced by the screening by trees of the chapel wing at the eastern end of the house; these remained in situ until the nineteenth century.<ref name=howard7/>

===18th century===
Chaloner Chute did not live to see his rebuilding completed. A century later, his descendant, John Chute, embarked on a process of "Gothicisation." In this process he was influenced by his friend [[Horace Walpole]], who had developed the innovative romantic Gothic style at his own country home, [[Strawberry Hill, London|Strawberry Hill]] in [[Twickenham]].{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=14}}

Many of the alterations and additions executed under Walpole's advice were replacements of old Tudor features which had been removed during the previous classical re-modelling, notably the battlements and towers. The chief alterations were to the chapel, and in the best romantic Gothic style, the creation of a tomb house adjoining it.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=78}} That the tomb house was dedicated to a man buried elsewhere and that no one was to be interred in a vault beneath was seen as no impediment to the creation of a mausoleum designed to enhance the [[Gothic fiction|Gothic atmosphere]] of the chapel and house.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=79}} Walpole, although the leading arbiter of good taste, was not allowed to have full control of the re-modelling and many of his suggestions for architectural reform at The Vyne went unheeded.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=78}}

===19th century===
During the 19th century, the house underwent minor changes and alterations. A sense of uniformity was given by the addition of [[bay window]]s to the two extending wings of the south front. This gave the unsymmetrical south front the classical cohesion it had hitherto lacked. Here, Walpole's influence is stronger than anywhere other in the mansion. At his instigation, towers were replaced by gables.{{citation needed|date=August 2022}} In 1842, William Wiggett, who sought to preserve the historic character of the house, acquired furniture and paintings related to John Chute at the sale of the estate of Horace Walpole at Strawberry Hill.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=80}}
[[James Austen]] was vicar of Sherborne St John and the Austen brothers were friends of the Chute family. They hunted with John Chute and the Austen family sometimes visited the Vyne.<ref name="Austenised">{{cite web|title=Austenised|url=https://austenised.blogspot.com/search/label/Mansfield%20Park}}{{better source|date=April 2024}}</ref>

== Interior ==

===Ground floor===

====The Chapel====
[[File:The antechapel at The Vyne.jpg|thumb|alt=A Tudor room, with dark wood-paneled walls and intricate ceiling woodwork, containing a number of paintings and pieces of furniture|The antechapel at The Vyne]]
The antechapel, one of the rooms still preserved in its medieval state, contains a painting of the Last Supper by [[Giovanni Domenico Ferretti]] which was requested from Horace Mann by Walpole on Chute's behalf.{{sfn|Tipping|1921|p=644}} It also contains fragments of stained glass from William Sandys' ruined [[Chapel of the Holy Ghost]] in Basingstoke.{{sfn|Tipping|1921|p=644}} The Tomb Chamber, a separate room adjacent to the chapel, was the largest of John Chute's Gothic amendments to the house, and houses a monument to Chaloner Chute designed in the classical style by [[Thomas Carter (sculptor)|Thomas Carter]].{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=79}} The chapel itself was built by William Sandys, replacing an earlier structure, and today retains the ribbed ceilings and intricately carved pews of the 16th century.{{sfn|Howard|Wilson|2003|p=89}}

====The Stone Gallery====
[[File:TheVyne12.jpg|thumb|Terracotta medallion of the Emperor Probus in the Stone Gallery.]]
The Stone Gallery occupies the entire space beneath the long gallery. The architectural historian, Mark Girouard, has advanced the theory that this gallery was originally an open loggia, a summer alternative to the indoor gallery above.<ref name=girouard100>Girouard, p. 100.</ref> If the Vyne's lower gallery was open, it would have been a precedent to the open gallery connecting the wings at [[Hatfield House]] which was built at the conclusion of the 16th century. What is known for sure is that it was already an enclosed gallery during the 18th century, however, its Tudor style ceiling is believed to date only from the 18th century, as does the gallery's Portland stone and marble floor.<ref>Howard, p. 17.</ref>

An important feature of the Stone Gallery is the terracotta medallion of the Emperor Probus which is inset above the fireplace. Made in Italy, probably by [[Giovanni da Maiano]], it is one of the oldest such medallions in Britain. Such medallions were to become a common external decorative feature during the short-lived English Renaissance period, similar medallions can be seen in the walls of Hampton Court Palace, while at [[Montacute House]], the former principal entrance has several circular recesses designed for such medallions which never materialised.<ref>Nicolson, p. 78.</ref> While it is possible this medallion may have decorated the walls of the Sandys grand mansion at The Vyne, there is no conclusive proof. It is not listed in an inventory of 1754 and there is speculation that John Chute acquired it following the demolition of the [[Palace of Whitehall|Whitehall's]] Holbein Gate.<ref>Howard, p. 18.</ref>

===First floor===
[[File:TheVyne7.jpg|thumb|The staircase is almost theatrical in its baroque [[chiaroscuro]] treatment of light, limited space and perspective.]]

The first floor is reached by an [[imperial staircase]]. At the centre of the house, it occupies a space once a hall in the original Tudor house. The staircase was built between 1769 and 1771. [[Horace Walpole]] had recommended its installation, however, John Chute eschewed Walpole's favoured Gothic and after a great deal of consideration of alternative styles designing himself a staircase in Palladian style.{{sfn|Worsley|1991|p=79}} The stairs are considered one of the notable features of the house. Taking every advantage of the comparatively small space confining them a single flight rises to a galleried half landing from which four further short flights rise to a colonnaded landings and galleries. The overall effect is almost theatrical in its treatment of light, space and perspective.<ref>Bullen, Crook, Hubbard, Pevsner, p. 533.</ref>

The Oak Gallery has been described as one of the most famous rooms in England.<ref name=Nicolson47/> it is remarkable because, as part of the Sandys mansion, it is believed to be one of the earliest [[long galleries]] in England,<ref name=girouard100/> likely to have been built in the 1520s.{{sfn|Coope|1986|p=50}} Within a few years of its completion, most Tudor mansions of note were to have such a room – used for entertaining, exercising and display, their very length became a matter of competition and pride and the dimensions of the long gallery at The Vyne were soon exceeded. The early date of the gallery, and its intended use as solely for exercise, is confirmed by the fact that it leads nowhere – one enters at the northern end and has no choice but to exit by the same door. Later galleries, such as that at Montacute had rooms leading off, almost as though they were corridors, while in other houses they would connect the house with a distant wing, chapel or even a church.<ref name=girouard100/>

The room is lined from floor to ceiling by over 400 linenfold panelling decorated with badges, crests and monograms. It seems though, that the Sandys display of their wealth in their long gallery was not as large as some of their contemporaries, an inventory of 1547, reports that the room was devoid of pictures and barely furnished.<ref>Girouard, p. 101.</ref>

The original mullioned windows have been replaced by classical sashes, however, the necessary cutting and alteration to the panelling during the alterations is not apparent. During the 19th century the panelling was coated with [[gesso]] and painted brown, this has been described as an "outrage".<ref name=nicolson46>Nicolson, p. 46.</ref> During the twentieth century, explorations into removing the paint were found to be not only too expensive, but liable to damage the panelling itself.<ref name=nicolson46/><ref>Howard. p. 13.</ref> In the mid-nineteenth century, the length of the room was slightly increased by the addition of a [[bay window]] at its southern end. At the same time the gallery was given a new floor and the rope patterned moulding on the plaster ceiling was given greater emphasis by a grained paint.

== Grounds ==
During the eighteenth century, the grounds were landscaped on the newly fashionable natural parkland style exemplified by the work of [[Capability Brown]] and later [[Humphrey Repton]]. A small stream, one of the headwaters of the [[Bow Brook, Hampshire|Bow Brook]], passing close to the house was dammed to form a lake.

3617261.extract: Selborne Common is a 99.6-hectare (246-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest west of Selborne in Hampshire. It is a Nature Conservation Review site, Grade I, and is part of the East Hampshire Hangers Special Area of Conservation. It is managed by the National Trust.

'''Selborne Common''' is a {{convert| 99.6 |ha|acre|abbr=off|adj=on}} biological [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] west of [[Selborne]] in [[Hampshire]].<ref name=dsv>{{cite web|url= https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/SiteDetail.aspx?SiteCode=S1003287&SiteName=&countyCode=19&responsiblePerson=&SeaArea=&IFCAArea=  |title=Designated Sites View:  Selborne Common | series= Sites of Special Scientific Interest|publisher=Natural England|accessdate = 18  May 2020}}</ref><ref name=map>{{cite web|url=https://magic.defra.gov.uk/MagicMap.aspx?startTopic=Designations&activelayer=sssiIndex&query=HYPERLINK%3D%271003287%27 |title=Map of Selborne Common|series= Sites of Special Scientific Interest|publisher=Natural England|accessdate= 18   May 2020}}</ref> It is a [[Nature Conservation Review]] site, Grade I,<ref>{{cite book|editor-first=Derek |editor-last=Ratcliffe  |title=A Nature Conservation Review|volume=2 |pages=52-53 |authorlink=Derek Ratcliffe |publisher= Cambridge University Press|location =Cambridge, UK  |year=1977|isbn= 0521 21403 3 }}</ref> and is part of the East Hampshire Hangers [[Special Area of Conservation]].<ref name=ehhsac>{{cite web|url= https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/SiteGeneralDetail.aspx?SiteCode=UK0012723&SiteName=&countyCode=19&responsiblePerson=&unitId=&SeaArea=&IFCAArea=  |title=Designated Sites View: East Hampshire Hangers  | series= Special Areas of Conservation|publisher=Natural England|accessdate =23   April 2020}}</ref> It is managed by the [[National Trust]].<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/combe-wood  |title= Coombe Wood  |publisher=National Trust| accessdate=  23  April 2020}}</ref>

==Topography==
The Common occupies the crown of [[Selborne Hill]], an easterly guardian of the [[Hampshire Downs]]. The highest part has an elevation of {{convert|680|ft}} above sea level. The southerly and westerly flanks slope away gently; on the other sides the contours are steeper. The steepest slope of all, with a maximum gradient of about 50%, overlooks the village and is called "Selborne Hanger". To the west of this is Coneycroft Hill, which in places is almost as precipitous. Between Selborne Hanger and Coneycroft Hill is a deep dell.

==Geology==
The soil on the Common consists of [[clay]] with [[flint]]s, overlying the [[chalk]] of which the South Downs are made. The watercourses are underground and discharge into the Oakhanger Stream, flowing north-eastwards, and the Caker Stream, flowing northwards. Both ultimately join the [[River Wey]].

==Flora==
The steepest slopes are clad in ancient [[European beech|beechwood]] (''Fagus sylvatica''): a "hanger", in East Hampshire, is just such a beechwood. The plateau is occupied by more beechwood, mixed with other broad-leaved species such as [[Pedunculate oak|English oak]] (''Quercus robur''), [[European ash|ash]] (''Fraxinus excelsior'') and [[Crataegus monogyna|hawthorn]] (''Crataegus monogyna''), and in places is scrubby. A small part of the plateau comprises open grassland with scattered [[Common gorse|gorse]] (''Ulex europaeus'') and stands of [[bracken]] (''Pteridium aquilinum''). Other, smaller areas of chalk grassland have recently been recreated elsewhere.

The Common is noted for its wild flowers, with thriving communities of [[yellow archangel]] (''Galeobdolon luteum''), [[wood spurge]] (''Euphorbia amygdaloides'') and [[Anemone nemorosa|wood anemone]] (''Anemone nemorosa''). [[Spurge-laurel]] (''Daphne laureola'') is sparsely but widely distributed. The Common is also home to such interesting species as [[stinking hellebore]] (''Helleborus foetidus''), [[green hellebore]] (''H. viridis'' ssp. ''occidentalis''), [[bird's nest orchid]] (''Neottia nidus-avis''), [[violet helleborine]] (''Epipactis purpurata''), the extreme rarity ''E.'' x ''schulzei'' (first British record here, 1931), and [[green-flowered helleborine]] (''E. phyllanthes'').

==Fauna==
Various rare molluscs and insects have been recorded. Butterflies on the Common include the [[Duke of Burgundy (butterfly)|Duke of Burgundy]] (''Hamearis lucina''), [[silver-washed fritillary]] (''Argynnis paphia'') and [[Apatura iris|purple emperor]] (''Apatura iris'').

The avifauna includes most of the species typical of broad-leaved woodland in southern England, such as [[Eurasian sparrowhawk|sparrowhawk]] (''Accipter nisus''), [[stock dove]] (''Columba oenas''), [[tawny owl]] (''Strix aluco''), [[European green woodpecker]] (''Picus viridis''), [[great spotted woodpecker]] (''Dendrocopos major''), [[garden warbler]] (''Sylvia borin''), [[blackcap]] (''S. atricapilla''), [[Common chiffchaff|chiffchaff]] (''Phylloscopus collybita''), [[spotted flycatcher]] (''Muscicapa striata''), [[marsh tit]] (''Parus palustris''), [[Eurasian nuthatch|nuthatch]] (''Sitta europaea''), [[Common treecreeper|treecreeper]] (''Certhia familiaris'') and [[Eurasian jay|jay]] (''Garrulus glandarius'').

[[Common buzzard|Buzzards]] (''Buteo buteo'') regularly hunt over the tree canopy. [[Eurasian hobby|Hobby]] (''Falco subbuteo''), [[woodcock]] (''Scolopax rusticola''), [[common firecrest]] (''Regulus ignicapillus'') and [[brambling]] (''Fringilla montifringilla'') are occasional visitors. Selborne Common is a reliable place to find the [[wood warbler]] (''Phylloscopus sibilatrix'').

[[Roe deer]] (''Capreolus capreolus'') and [[Hazel dormouse|dormouse]] (''Muscardinus avellanarius'') are resident mammals.

==History and management==
From the prehistoric or Romano-British period there is evidence of a [[field system]], which may have been re-used during the [[Middle Ages]]. The Common has not been ploughed since then.

Earthworks on the western boundary have tentatively been dated to the mid thirteenth century, when Newton Park was emparked. An earth bank, running across the Common, has been dated to around 1750 and was probably used to protect [[Coppicing|coppice]] woodland from grazing animals.

During the eighteenth century, the [[lord of the manor]] felled beeches on the Common. Local people exercised their [[Common land|common rights]] to graze cattle and sheep and to collect firewood, activities which continued into the 1950s.

In mediaeval times the nearby [[Selborne Priory]] was lord of the manor of Selborne; the manor subsequently passed to [[Magdalen College, Oxford]], which donated it to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in 1932. Cattle have recently been reintroduced in an attempt to reconstruct the ancient, flower-rich, wood-pasture habitat which commoning produced and which has almost disappeared from England.

A [[dew pond]], Wood Pond, is situated near the western boundary.

==Gilbert White==
Selborne Common is internationally famous for its association with the eighteenth-century naturalist, [[Gilbert White]].

==Access==
The Common is freely accessible to all, subject to the National Trust's byelaws. It is best approached from Selborne, via the (steep) Zig-Zag or Bostal paths (car park behind the Selborne Arms public house, Ordnance Survey reference {{gbmappingsmall|SU742335}}). A more level track leads to the Common from [[Newton Valence]]; footpaths join it also from the south-east and north-west. After rain and especially in winter, some paths can become very muddy.

Selborne Common is on the [[Hangers Way]].

3642198.title: Sandham Memorial Chapel
3642198.extract:
Sandham Memorial Chapel is in the village of Burghclere, Hampshire, England. It is a Grade I listed, 1920s decorated chapel, designed by Lionel Pearson. The chapel was built to accommodate a series of paintings by the English artist Stanley Spencer. It was commissioned by Mary and John Louis Behrend (1881–1972) as a memorial to Mary's brother, Lieutenant Henry Willoughby Sandham who died of illness contracted in Macedonia after the First World War.  The chapel is surrounded by lawns and orchards, with views of Watership Down.
It is run by the National Trust and is open to the public.

'''Sandham Memorial Chapel''' is in the village of [[Burghclere]], [[Hampshire]], England. It is a Grade I [[listed building|listed]],<ref name="Listing">{{National Heritage List for England |num=1339741  |desc=Sandham Memorial Chapel|accessdate=1 October 2016}}</ref> 1920s decorated chapel, designed by [[Lionel Pearson]]. The chapel was built to accommodate a series of paintings by the English artist [[Stanley Spencer]]. It was commissioned by Mary and John Louis Behrend (1881–1972) as a memorial to Mary's brother, Lieutenant Henry Willoughby Sandham who died of illness contracted in Macedonia after the [[World War I|First World War]].  The chapel is surrounded by lawns and orchards, with views of [[Watership Down, Hampshire|Watership Down]].

It is run by the [[National Trust]] and is open to the public.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/sandham-memorial-chapel/|title=Sandham Memorial Chapel|publisher=[[National Trust]]|accessdate=1 October 2016}}</ref>

== Paintings ==

Spencer's series of seventeen paintings was inspired by his own experiences during the First World War, in which he served as an orderly with the [[Royal Army Medical Corps]], first at [[Beaufort War Hospital]] in Bristol, and then on the [[Macedonian front]], where he was subsequently transferred to the infantry.<ref>Gough (2006). ''Journey to Burghclere''. p.73.</ref> He was influenced by [[Giotto]]’s [[Arena Chapel]] murals in [[Padua]]. He wanted to paint [[fresco]]es too, but the environmental conditions were not appropriate. Upon being commissioned to paint the murals for the chapel, Spencer was heard to exclaim “What Ho, Giotto!” <ref>{{cite web|title=Paul Gough The Holy Box|url=https://pallantbookshop.com/product/the-holy-box/}}</ref> 
The subsequent paintings were commissioned in 1923, with Spencer moving to Burghclere in 1926 to work ''in situ''. The series was completed in 1932. It is dominated by the [[Resurrection]] scene behind the altar, in which dozens of British soldiers lay the white wooden crosses that marked their graves at the feet of a distant Christ. The series chronicles Spencer's everyday experiences of the war rather than any scenes of action. When the art historian [[R. H. Wilenski]] saw the recently completed sequence, he wrote of his sense "that every one of the thousand memories recorded had been driven into the artist's consciousness like a sharp-pointed nail".<ref>Haycock (2009). ''A Crisis of Brilliance''. p. 331.</ref>

== Name ==

The Chapel is consecrated as '''The Oratory of All Saints''' and only became officially recognised by its colloquial name Sandham Memorial Chapel following the National Trust's takeover of the property. Spencer would refer to it as his "Holy-Box", whilst the architect and patrons would privately refer to it as Spencer's "God-Box". Meanwhile, John and Mary Behrend's children pejoratively called it the "biscuit factory", in response to its "municipal" characteristics.<ref>Bromwell (2014). ''The God-Box of Burghclere'', p. 58.</ref>

The '''Winchester City Mill''' is a restored [[watermill|water mill]] situated on the [[River Itchen, Hampshire|River Itchen]] in the centre of the ancient [[England|English]] city of [[Winchester]]. The mill is owned by the [[National Trust]] and is a Grade II* [[listed building]].<ref>{{cite web|title=1 Water Lane, Winchester|url=https://www.historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1095347|website=Historic England|accessdate=25 May 2018}}</ref>

==History==
The mill was recorded, milling [[cereal|corn]], in the [[Domesday Book]] of 1086.  However, there are earlier references going back to 932 in the [[Winchester Cathedral|cathedral]] records. In 989 Queen [[Ælfthryth (wife of Edgar)]], had passed the mill to the nuns of [[Wherwell Abbey]]. [[Dendrochronology|Dendrochronological]] measurements date some of the timbers to the 11th Century.<ref>{{cite journal |title=City Mill, Winchester |journal=Newsletter|date=Autumn 2018|issue=122|url=https://www.hampshiremills.org/Newsletters/122%20Autumn%2018%20Newsletter/122%20Page%206.htm |publisher=Hampshire Mills Group |accessdate=2 August 2019|first=Ruth|last=Andrews}}</ref>

It was originally known as Eastgate Mill because it lay just outside the east gate of the city of Winchester, but was renamed City Mill when it was given to the city by [[Mary I of England|Mary I]] following her marriage to [[Philip II of Spain]] at Winchester Cathedral in 1554<ref name="NT">{{cite book|title=The City Mill, Winchester|publisher=National Trust}}</ref> The mill was last rebuilt in 1744 by James Cook, a tanner. A sketch made by the artist [[J. M. W. Turner]] in 1795 shows that the building and millraces today are relatively unchanged.<ref name="NT" />

In 1820 the Corporation sold the mill to John Benham whose family owned the mill until the early 1900s. During the late 1890s, City Mill struggled financially owing to competition from adjacent mills at Durngate<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reynolds |first=J |date=1967 |title=Durngate Mill, Winchester |url=https://www.hantsfieldclub.org.uk/publications/hampshirestudies/digital/1960s/vol24/Reynolds&others.pdf |journal=Proceedings of the Hampshire Field Club and Archaeological Society |volume=24 |pages=103}}</ref> and Wharf Hill,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gregory |first=M |date=2020 |title=Wharf Mill (Segrim's Mill), Winchester |url=https://www.hias.org.uk/Journal%20scans/HIAS%20Journal%202020.pdf |journal=Hampshire Industrial Archaeology Society Journal |volume=28 |pages=17–22}}</ref> and had ceased operation by 1910.  The mill was used as a [[laundry]] during [[World War I]], then became derelict. In 1928 the building was at risk of demolition;<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/hampshire/winchester-city-mill/the-history-of-winchester-city-mill|title=The history of Winchester City Mill|website=National trust|accessdate=12 October 2024}}</ref> but it was saved by a group of benefactors who bought the mill and presented it to the National Trust. In 1931 the mill was leased to the [[Youth Hostels Association (England & Wales)|Youth Hostels Association]] for use as a [[hostel]], a usage that continued until 2005.<ref name="NT" />

{{for|an explanation of the various pieces of machinery|Mill machinery}}
In 2004, a 12-year restoration program came to a successful conclusion, and after a hiatus of at least 90 years the mill again milled flour by water power. The water wheel has subsequently been run daily throughout the year with flour milling demonstrations at weekends. The mill building also houses a National Trust café and shop.<ref>{{cite web |title=Facilities and access |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/winchester-city-mill#Facilities%20and%20access |website=National Trust |access-date=3 July 2022}}</ref>

==Otter Watch==
In partnership with the [[Hampshire and Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust]] and the [[Environment Agency]], night-vision cameras have been set up to monitor the river passing under the mill and record images of [[Eurasian otter|otters]] passing through.  Recordings of sightings are played back on a monitor in the stone floor area.<ref>{{cite book|title=Welcome to Winchester City Mill|publisher=National Trust}}</ref>

'''Hinton Ampner''' is a village and country house estate with gardens and former [[civil parish]], now in the parish of [[Bramdean and Hinton Ampner]], in the [[City of Winchester|Winchester]] district, in the county of [[Hampshire]], England. It is near [[New Alresford|Alresford]] and eight miles due east of [[Winchester]].{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=1}} The village lies on the north slope of a long chalk ridge, with the house and church at its highest point.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=17}} The area is part of the broader [[Hampshire Downs]], a large area of predominantly chalk downland. The nearest large river is the [[River Itchen, Hampshire|River Itchen]] to the west of the area. To the north west of Hinton is the village of [[Cheriton, Hampshire|Cheriton and New Cheriton]]. The village of [[Kilmeston]] is to the south.

The house is a Grade II [[listed building]].<ref>{{NHLE|grade=II|desc=Hinton Ampner House|num=1095121|date=5 December 1955}}</ref> The house and garden are owned by the [[National Trust]] and are open to the public.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hinton Ampner |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/hinton-ampner |publisher=The National Trust |access-date=27 June 2020}}</ref><ref>''Hinton Ampner''. The National Trust, 2008. {{ISBN|978-1-84359-291-4}}</ref>

==Etymology==
{{See also|Hinton (place name)}}

The name derives from the old English ''hēah tūn'' meaning the homestead on the high ground. The suffix ''Ampner'' is a [[Language change|corruption]] of ''Almoner'', denoting that an [[Almoner]] of [[Winchester Cathedral Priory|St. Swithuns Priory]] owned the manor.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=16}}<ref>E. Ekwall; Dictionary of English Place-Names, 241</ref>

==History==
The area around Hinton has evidence of [[Neolithic]] and [[Bronze Age]] activity, including the presence of several barrows.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=12}} The first record of the village was in the [[Domesday]] survey of 1086 which recorded 8 [[Hide (unit)|Hides]] and a church.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=12}}

In 1931 the parish had a population of 330.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://visionofbritain.org.uk/unit/10092565/cube/TOT_POP|title=Population statistics Hinton Ampner AP/CP through time|publisher=[[A Vision of Britain through Time]]|accessdate=18 May 2023}}</ref> On 1 April 1932 the parish was abolished and merged with Bramdean.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://visionofbritain.org.uk/unit/10092565|title=Relationships and changes Hinton Ampner AP/CP through time|publisher=A Vision of Britain through Time|accessdate=18 May 2023}}</ref>

==Church==
[[File:All Saints Church, Hinton Ampner.jpg|thumb|right|All Saints Church, Hinton Ampner, seen from the south.]]
The local church, All Saints Church, lies between the manor house and village cottages. {{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=17}} The current church dates mostly from the 13th century but incorporates some pre-[[Norman Conquest]] elements from a previous church.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=22}} The church was altered in the early 19th century and the bell tower modified.{{sfn|Tinniswood|2020|p=43}} The church contains numerous memorials to the previous owners of the estate, as well as three historic bells, two dated 1603 and the other 1719.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=27}} The church also contains several items and memorials rescued by Ralph Dutton from the church of St.Mary at [[Laverstoke]] which was demolished in the early 1950s.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=27}} Dutton also commissioned two windows for the east end, designed by [[Patrick Reyntiens]] and [[John Piper (artist)|John Piper]] in 1970.{{sfn|Tinniswood|2020|p=43}} All Saints is a Grade II* [[listed building]].<ref name=NHLE>{{NHLE|grade=II*|desc=Church of All Saints|num=1155865|date=5 December 1955}}</ref>

==Hinton Ampner House==
In the 1540s, a large [[Tudor architecture|Tudor]] manor house was built in Hinton Ampner.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=33}} By 1597, the house was under the ownership of the [[Stewkley baronets|Stewkley family]], when Thomas Stewkley took over the lease from the Dean and Chapter of Winchester.{{sfn|Hussey|1947|p=327}} In 1719, on the death of Sir Hugh Stewkley, the estate passed to his daughter Mary who married Edward Stawell.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=42}} Their descendant, [[Henry Bilson-Legge, 2nd Baron Stawell|Henry Stawell Bilson-Legge]] subsequently inherited the estate and demolished the Tudor house in favour of a new building (the old house being on the site of the present day orchard).{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=53}}

The current Hinton Ampner house was built in 1793 and remodelled extensively in 1867.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=16}} The house passed into the Dutton family in 1803 when Hampshire heiress Mary Bilson-Legge married [[John Dutton, 2nd Baron Sherborne|John Dutton]], who later became 2nd Lord Sherborne.{{sfn|Tinniswood|2020|p=6}} It passed to their second son, John Dutton, whose descendants owned the estate until it passed to the National Trust.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=60}} [[Ralph Dutton, 8th Baron Sherborne|Ralph Dutton]], its final owner, inherited the estate upon the death of his father in 1935{{sfn|Richardson|2008|p=131}} and quickly proceeded to transform the Victorian design and décor, which he detested.{{sfn|Richardson|2008|p=133}} The house was remodelled in the [[Georgian architecture#Post-Georgian developments|Neo-Georgian]] style by Trenwith Wills and [[Gerald Wellesley, 7th Duke of Wellington|Lord Gerald Wellesley]] for Ralph Dutton between 1936 and 1939 to his vision of what it would have been like had it been built on its current scale in 1790 – a Georgian country house.<ref>{{cite journal|first=Dan|last=Cruickshank|author-link=Dan Cruickshank|title=Wills and Wellesley|journal=National Trust Magazine|page=38|date=Summer 2012}}</ref>

[[File:Hinton Ampner North Side.jpg|thumb|right|The north facing main entrance of the house]]
During the [[Second World War]], the house was used as accommodation for girls from the [[Portsmouth High School, Southsea|Portsmouth Girls School]] to keep them away from the city.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=87}} The house was badly damaged by fire in April 1960, with nearly all rooms impacted by fire or smoke.{{sfn|Hussey|1965|p=1424}} A restoration campaign was initiated within days of the fire, led by the same firm that had undertaken the renovations in the 1930s.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=97}} The work was completed in May 1963, including the alteration of the roof line, which returned the building to its Georgian dimensions.{{sfn|Hussey|1965|p=1424}} Dutton decorated the house with many pieces recycled from stately homes{{sfn|Tinniswood|2020|p=15}} and worked with designer [[Ronald Fleming (interior decorator)|Ronald Fleming]] to decorate the rooms in a manner appropriate to his rebuilt collection.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=101}}

Ralph Dutton, with no direct heirs, gave the estate to the National Trust, on his death in 1985.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=3}} He is buried in the graveyard of the nearby church of All Saints.{{sfn|Tinniswood|2020|p=43}}

===Interior and collections===
Long before inheriting the house, Ralph Dutton became an avid collector of early 18th century furnishings and the house is now lavishly decorated with notable examples of Regency art and decorative objects.{{sfn|Hussey|1947|p=328}} Dutton's acquisitions were in part funded by his literary efforts, having written a series of books on architecture and history.{{sfn|Tinniswood|2020|p=7}}

====The entrance hall====
A notable feature of the entrance hall is the [[Porphyry (geology)|porphyry]] fireplace, salvaged by Dutton from [[Hamilton Palace]],{{sfn|Hussey|1947|p=328}} over which hangs ''Selene and Endymion'' by [[Giovanni Antonio Pellegrini]].{{sfn|Tinniswood|2020|p=14}} The giltwood [[torchère]]s were purchased from the 1949 sale at [[Tortworth Court]].{{sfn|Tinniswood|2020|p=14}}

====The dining room====
[[File:The dining room at Hinton Ampner.jpg|thumb|upright|alt=An 18th century dining room with a long table holding an array of ceramics, silverware and glassware. |The dining room]]
A reproduction of a ceiling by [[Robert Adam]], originally designed for [[Robert Child (Wells MP)|Robert Child]] of [[Osterley Park|Osterley]] but due to be demolished at Lord Rosebury's house at 38 Berkeley Square in London, was recreated in the dining room.{{sfn|Hussey|1965|p=1428}} This involved detaching the original painted paper roundels by [[Angelica Kauffman]] and taking moulds of Adam's plasterwork. The work was completed in 1940 but later largely destroyed, including all Kauffman's work, by the 1960 fire.<ref name=NTG>{{cite book |last1=Rowell |first1=Christopher |title=Hinton Ampner |date=1988 |publisher=National Trust |location=Swindon |page=26}}</ref> Dutton hired Elizabeth Biddulph [[Royal Institute of Oil Painters|ROI]]<ref>{{cite book |last1=Buckman |first1=David |title=Artists in Britain since 1945 |date=2006 |publisher=Art Dictionaries |location=Bristol |isbn=9780953260959 |page=136}}</ref> to repaint all of the roundels.{{sfn|Hussey|1965|p=1427}} The mirror, also a design by Robert Adam, was originally designed for Derby House in [[Grosvenor Square]].{{sfn|Hussey|1965|p=1427}} Also notable is a pair of paintings, probably from an original set of the four seasons in the manner of [[Jacob de Wit]], depicting [[putti]] painted in a three-dimensional [[grisaille]] style.<ref name=NTG />

====The library====
[[File:The library at Hinton Ampner.jpg|thumb|alt=A library decorated with 18th century art and furniture, with books lining the walls|The library]]
Dutton's book collection was completely destroyed in the 1960 fire and was completely replaced with newly acquired works.{{sfn|Hussey|1965|p=1427}} The marble and porphyry fireplace, decorated with [[Napoleon]]'s insignia, may have come from the [[Château de Saint-Cloud]].{{sfn|Hussey|1965|p=1427}} Hanging over the fireplace is ''Esther Fainting Before Ahasuerus'' by [[Francesco Fontebasso]].{{sfn|Tinniswood|2020|p=8}}

===Poltergeist claims===
The old Tudor house attained notoriety, in the 18th century, after it was said to have become uninhabitable due to loud noises attributed to a [[poltergeist]]. One tenant, Mary Ricketts, wrote about her experiences in the house,<ref>{{Cite book|title = A Natural History of Ghosts|last = Clarke|first = Roger|publisher = Particular Books|year = 2012|isbn = 978-1-846-14333-5|pages = 35–69}}</ref> which included mysterious sounds as well as ghostly figures.{{sfn|Hussey|1947|p=327}} That house was pulled down in 1793, after its replacement had been built about {{convert|50|m|ft|abbr=off}} to the south.{{sfn|Dutton|1988|p=16}} [[Harry Price]], citing Ricketts' statements, wrote at length about the case in his book ''Poltergeist Over England'' (1945).

Claims about the poltergeist were disputed by [[Trevor H. Hall]] who suggested that "underground water was mainly responsible for the noises at Hinton, although the account of some of them is highly suggestive of seismic disturbance."<ref>Hall, Trevor H. (1958). ''Four Modern Ghosts''. Duckworth. p. 22</ref>

===The gardens===
[[File:Yew Path, Hinton Ampner.jpg|thumb|Yew Path, Hinton Ampner]]
The current garden layout of the house was created by Ralph Dutton, starting in 1930, making this a modern 20th-century garden.<ref>{{cite web |title=The garden at Hinton Ampner |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/hinton-ampner/features/the-garden-at-hinton-ampner |publisher=The National Trust |access-date=27 June 2020}}</ref> Previously, the parkland came directly up to the house, which was designed to be a hunting lodge. He redeveloped the gardens, creating a lily pond along the east façade of the house, as well as replanting the terraces to the south.{{sfn|Tinniswood|2020|p=32}} The formal gardens are particularly notable for the variety of roses.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schramm |first1=Darrell |title=Roses at Hinton Ampner |journal=American Rose |date=2015 |volume=43 |issue=6 |pages=90–93}}</ref> The estate in total comprises {{convert|667|ha|abbr=off}} of chalk farm and woodland, replanted by Dutton, which were included in the 1985 bequest to the National Trust.{{sfn|Brooks|Garnett|2000|p=47}}

}}'''West Green House''' is an 18th-century [[country house]] and garden at West Green in [[Hartley Wintney]] in the [[England|English]] county of [[Hampshire]]. The house is [[Listed building#Categories of listed building|listed Grade II*]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=WEST GREEN HOUSE, Hartley Wintney - 1242807 {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1242807 |access-date=2022-03-21 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}}</ref> It is known for its gardens and for its summer season of [[opera]].

==History==
[[File:West Green House England - 54297276752.jpg|left|thumb|West Green House Garden]]
The house was built around 1714–1720,<ref name="EH">{{NHLE |num=1242807 |desc=West Green House |accessdate=12 February 2015}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=History |url=https://www.westgreenhouse.co.uk/garden/history/ |access-date=25 April 2026 |website=West Green House Gardens |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=West Green House |url=https://research.hgt.org.uk/item/west-green-house/ |access-date=25 April 2026 |website=Hampshire Gardens Trust}}</ref> by General [[Henry Hawley]], who led the cavalry charge at the [[Battle of Culloden]].<ref name="Keiller1999">{{cite book |author=Patrick Keiller|title=Robinson in Space: And a Conversation With Patrick Wright |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zG1lgCyA19gC&pg=PA11 |accessdate=6 January 2013|year=1999 |publisher=Reaktion Books |isbn=978-1-86189-028-3 |pages=11–}}</ref>

At the beginning of the 20th century the Playfair family employed the architect [[Robert Weir Schulz]] to remodel the north front of the house and to design new gardens.<ref name="Sisley">{{cite web| url=https://www.sisley.co.uk/west-green-house/|title=English gardens - West Green Houses|publisher=Sisley Garden Tours| accessdate=6 January 2013}}</ref> After the Playfairs left West Green House five years later, the new owner, Evelyn, Duchess of Wellington continued to improve the gardens.<ref name="Sisley"/> The Duchess and her friend Yvonne Fitzroy occupied the house and garden for many years. [[Victor Sassoon]] bought the house and allowed the Duchess and her friend to live in house until the Duchess's death in 1939 and Fitzroy's death in 1971.<ref name="Sisley"/>

The [[National Trust]] has owned the house since 1971, after being left the property by Victor Sassoon in 1957. [[Alistair McAlpine, Baron McAlpine of West Green|Alistair McAlpine]] acquired the lease in 1976 and added monuments designed by the classical architect [[Quinlan Terry]].<ref name="Taylor2008">{{cite book |author=Patrick Taylor|title=Gardens of Britain and Ireland|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=D5u4y832PZYC&pg=PA108|accessdate=6 January 2013 |date=1 May 2008 |publisher=Dorling Kindersley|isbn=978-1-4053-2854-8|pages=108–}}</ref>

The house was damaged by an [[Irish Republican Army|IRA]] bomb attack in 1990.<ref name="LAIRA">{{cite web| url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-06-16-mn-106-story.html|title=IRA Claims Blame in Wave of Blasts|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=6 January 2013}}</ref> McAlpine had left the house three weeks previously, at the expiration of his lease.<ref name="LAIRA"/>

Marylyn Abbott bought the lease from the National Trust in 1993.<ref name=KT>{{cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052702303823104576391250165901330 |title=Music Inhabits Summer Gardens |last=Kirwan-Taylor |first=Helen |newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |date=1 July 2011 |accessdate=23 July 2013 }}</ref> She had previously developed her well-known [[Kennerton Green]] garden in [[Mittagong, New South Wales]], Australia.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/country--garden-the-colour-of-two-continents-1130105.html |title=Country & garden: The colour of two continents |last=Pavord |first=Anna |newspaper=[[The Independent]] |date=4 December 1999 |accessdate=23 July 2013 }}</ref> The gardens at West Green house now extends beyond the 18th century walls to beyond a lake created in 1997 which is surrounded by a series of perimeter gardens, one a fountain “ Paradise Garden”, another a 190 meter serpentine of iris crossed by five wisteria clad bridges. With six walled gardens, each individually planted from checkerboard topiary, to tropical plants in summer, and oriental plants around two dragons, it is a garden known for its theatricality.{{cn|date= March 2024}} Alongside the garden, there is a gift-shop and cafe.

==Opera==
Marylyn Abbott is the former marketing and tourism manager of [[Sydney Opera House]]<ref name=KT/> and instituted an opera season at West Green House which is held annually in July and August.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.standard.co.uk/goingout/music/best-garden-operas-in-london-6471057.html |title=Best garden operas in London |last=Kimberley |first=Nick |newspaper=[[London Evening Standard]] |date=19 May 2010 |accessdate=23 July 2013 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140106054353/http://www.standard.co.uk/goingout/music/best-garden-operas-in-london-6471057.html |archivedate=6 January 2014 }}</ref> Today the opera is performed from a stage cantilevered from the lake's island with the audience seated in covered pavilions lake side.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/open-gardens/8645647/The-perfect-setting-for-outdoor-opera.html |title=The perfect setting for outdoor opera |last=Raymond |first=Francine |newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |date=19 July 2011 |accessdate=23 July 2013 }}</ref> 

In 2012, West Green House hosted a production by the [[Garsington Opera]] Emerging Artists programme.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://blogs.telegraph.co.uk/culture/michaelwhite/100065427/a-country-house-academy-for-opera-singers-the-new-venture-between-garsington-and-west-green-house/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120804005405/http://blogs.telegraph.co.uk/culture/michaelwhite/100065427/a-country-house-academy-for-opera-singers-the-new-venture-between-garsington-and-west-green-house/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=4 August 2012 |title=A country-house academy for opera singers |last=White |first=Michael |newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |date=1 August 2012 |accessdate=23 July 2013 }}</ref>

{{Short description|Nature reserve in Hampshire, England}}
[[File:Waggoners Wells - geograph.org.uk - 1297098.jpg|thumb|The middle pond, Waggoners Wells|alt=part of a lake with greenish water with beech trees in leaf beyond]]
'''Ludshott Common and Waggoners Wells''' (the latter sometimes written with an apostrophe: Waggoners' Wells) is a [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] reserve; Ludshott Common is an area of heathland and Waggoners Wells a series of man-made ponds with a connecting stream. The reserve is situated between [[Grayshott]], [[Bramshott]] and [[Headley Down]] in [[East Hampshire]], [[England]]. To the south is the large heathland area of [[Bramshott Common]].<ref>Ordnance Survey</ref> Some {{convert|415|acre|ha}} is under the care of the [[Woodland Trust]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Woodland Trust: Ludshott Common and Waggoners Wells|url=https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/visiting-woods/woods/ludshott-common-and-waggoners-wells/|access-date=6 March 2023}}</ref>

==Ludshott Common==
===Description===
Ludshott Common is one of the largest remaining areas of [[heathland]] in [[East Hampshire]].<ref>{{cite web|title=National Trust - Ludshott Commons|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/ludshott-commons/|accessdate=2 Mar 2014}}</ref> It lies parallel to and south of the B3002 road between Headley Down to the west and Grayshott to the east. It covers {{convert|285|ha|acre}} and is designated a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI) and [[Special Protection Area]] (SPA) due to the number of endangered species, including [[woodlark]], [[nightjar]] and [[Dartford warbler]]. There are also a great many spiders and butterflies, including [[silver-studded blue]], [[grayling (butterfly)|grayling]] and [[green hairstreak]].<ref>{{cite web|title=National Trust: Ludshott Commons|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/ludshott-commons|access-date=14 September 2021}}</ref><ref name=NTludshott>[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-global/w-localtoyou/w-thames_solent/w-thames_solent-countryside/w-south_east-places-west_weald-ludshott.htm National Trust | South East | Ludshott Common & Waggoner's Wells] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090917192641/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-global/w-localtoyou/w-thames_solent/w-thames_solent-countryside/w-south_east-places-west_weald-ludshott.htm |date=2009-09-17 }}</ref> [[Vipera berus|Adders]], [[grass snake]]s and [[sand lizard]]s also inhabit the common.<ref>{{cite web|title=National Trust: Ludshott: Reptiles|url=http://www.ntludshott.org.uk/#!reptiles/c2170|accessdate=11 Mar 2014}}</ref> Rabbits are widespread and roe deer may occasionally be seen.<ref>{{cite web|title=National Trust: Ludshott: Animals|url=http://www.ntludshott.org.uk/#!animals/c20eb|accessdate=11 Mar 2014}}</ref> The most common trees are [[Scots pine]] and [[silver birch]], with some oak.

While much of the common is heather and gorse scrub on a fine sandy soil, there was an elevated stand of mature Scots pine trees with little or no undergrowth known locally as "the cathedral" or "cathedral pines".<ref>{{cite web|title=Ludshott Common cathedral|url=https://www.geograph.org.uk/search.php?i=47390530|accessdate=3 Mar 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=National Trust: Commons Link newsletter|url=http://media.wix.com/ugd/ac7904_885d427bd123e354cd2464fd679a11b5.pdf|accessdate=3 Mar 2014}}</ref> Many had been removed by the end of 2020, owing to their roots having been damaged by fires.<ref>{{cite web|title=Headley History timeline|url=http://www.johnowensmith.co.uk/headley/calendar.htm|access-date=14 September 2021}}</ref>

In 2013 consultations were underway with a view to seeking permission to resume grazing on 550 acres of the common.<ref>{{cite web|title=National Trust: Ludshott: Grazing|url=http://www.ntludshott.org.uk/#!grazing/c1mmc|accessdate=11 Mar 2014}}</ref>

===History===
'''Ludshott Common''' constituted half of the ancient Manor of Ludshott, in the [[Hundred (county division)|Hundred]] of [[Neatham Hundred|Neatham]], dating back to Saxon times. It is described as being under the lordship of [[Hugh de Port]] in the [[Domesday Book]] of 1086, where it was listed as comprising 10 households; in 1066 the overlord had been King [[Edward the Confessor]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Open Domesday: Ludshott|url=https://opendomesday.org/place/SU8434/ludshott/|accessdate=16 October 2021}}</ref> [[Manorial roll|Court baron rolls]] go back to about 1400.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ludshott Manor Court Rolls|url=http://www.johnowensmith.co.uk/headley/ludshott1intro.htm|accessdate=11 Mar 2014}}</ref>

Ludshott Common owes its present state to the traditional use made of [[common land]] by local people: to graze their cattle, pigs, sheep, and ponies and to collect gorse, heather, wood, and bracken for fuel, and for animal bedding and winter fodder. Such uses ceased around the beginning of the 20th century. The land was acquired by the National Trust in 1908 in response to the growing pressure from housing development in Headley Down.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ludshott Common in the 20th century|url=http://headley-village.com/interactive/book/export/html/66|accessdate=2 Mar 2014}}</ref>

During the Second World War in the 1940s, Ludshott Common was used as a tank manoeuvres training ground, and the heather was largely turned to mud. The heather recovered, and was managed from the 1970s onwards. A camp (named Superior Camp) for Canadian troops, one of several in the vicinity, was built at the eastern corner of the common. Evidence of the layout can be seen even though it was demolished in the 1950s/1960s.

Periodically, fires would break out on the common. In 1962, {{convert|200|acre|km2}} were burnt and, in 1965, {{convert|400|acre|km2}}. Further serious fires occurred in 1969 and 1976, the latter being the worst ever known in Hampshire, spreading rapidly and burning {{convert|600|acre|km2}}, lasting eight days. On 12 May 1980, 600 of the {{convert|695|acre|km2}} were burnt by a fire fanned by high winds. Residents of roads in Headley Down which bordered the common were evacuated. Firefighters brought the fire under control in just over seven hours at 19:55. Relief crews remained on site overnight controlling small outbreaks of fire and damping down, with further relief crews taking over at 06:00 the following morning.<ref>The History of Grayshott Fire Station 1906 - 2007, Hampshire Fire & Rescue, 2007.</ref>

==Waggoners Wells==
[[File:National Trust wishing well sign, Waggoners Wells, Grayshott.jpg|thumb|Wishing well plaque commemorating composition of [[Flower in the Crannied Wall]]]]
'''Waggoners Wells''' is set amongst woodland in a steep valley situated between Ludshott Common to the north west and [[Bramshott Common]] to the south east.

The original name of the series of ponds was Wakeners' Wells. They were created in the 17th century by the Hooke family of Bramshott. <ref>Grayshott Village Archive - [https://web.archive.org/web/20070718013929/http://www.grayshott-archive.org.uk/articles/history_of_grayshott.html History of Grayshott] (via [[Internet Archive]])</ref> They were possibly originally intended as hammer ponds, that is, to serve the local iron industry, but they appear never to have been so used.<ref name="NTludshott" /> The woodland surrounding the ponds is notable for its mature beech trees.

Vehicular access is via Waggoners Wells Lane from Grayshott as far as the ford and a small car park beyond; the lane originally continued south-eastwards to Kingswood Lane, and thence to the London to Portsmouth road ([[A3 road|A3]]), but today only a footpath through the woodland remains.

[[Catch and release]] fishing for carp, roach, tench, perch and other species is a popular pursuit,<ref>{{cite web|title=Grayshott Angling Club: Waggoners Wells|url=http://home.btconnect.com/grayshottanglingclub/|accessdate=3 Mar 2014}} (Details and photographs)</ref> as is nature rambling and birdwatching.

[[File:"Summerden" on Waggoners Wells - geograph.org.uk - 1160317.jpg|thumb|Summerden|alt=four-bay red-brick two-storey house with roof dormers]]
The stream that emerges from the pond furthest to the south-west is called Cooper's Stream. The house situated at the bottom of the ponds is Summerden and is a private residence of the National Trust warden of the area. Near it is a wishing well, mentioned by [[Flora Thompson]] in her writings of the locality, and recorded by a National Trust plaque as being the place at which [[Alfred, Lord Tennyson]] was inspired to compose his short poem [[Flower in the Crannied Wall]]. The stream flowing from Waggoners Wells runs west to [[Standford]], around the west of [[Headley, East Hampshire|Headley]], and eventually into the [[River Wey]]. The stream powered many mills that worked ironworks, including [[Headley Water Mill|Headley Mill]]. Paper mills were also run along the water that flowed from Waggoners Wells.

The gatefold photo of [[Fleetwood Mac]]'s 1973 album ''[[Penguin (album)|Penguin]]'' was shot on location at Waggoners Wells.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.fleetwoodmac.net/penguin/qa/davewalker_qa1.htm |title=Dave Walker Q&A; Session, October 2000 |access-date=2017-01-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161031113234/http://www.fleetwoodmac.net/penguin/qa/davewalker_qa1.htm |archive-date=2016-10-31 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

64003988.title: Stockbridge Common Marsh
64003988.extract:
Stockbridge Common Marsh is a 64.8-hectare (160-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest south of Stockbridge in Hampshire. It is owned by the National Trust.
This site stretches for 2 kilometres (1.2 miles) along the flood plain of the River Test. It has wetland habitats including marsh, fen, carr, alluvial meadows and a large shallow lake. The marsh has a rich variety of flora, with 180 species of flowering plants, including bog pimpernel, adder’s-tongue fern,  marsh  valerian and bogbean.

64005266.title: Stockbridge Down
64005266.extract:
Stockbridge Down is a 69.8-hectare (172-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest east of Stockbridge in Hampshire. It is a Nature Conservation Review site, Grade 2. It is owned by the National Trust and parts of it are designated as scheduled monuments, including an Iron Age hillfort (Woolbury) and fourteen Bronze Age burial mounds.
This site has a variety of scrub and grassland habitats on a north-west facing slope of chalk and a clay-with-flints plateau. There is a diverse range of butterflies, such as chalk-hill blue, marbled white and dark green fritillary, while moths include the oblique striped.
